Much of the humus in most soils has persisted for more than 100 years rather than having been decomposed into CO.
The long-persisting humus in most soils can be regarded as stable.
Much of the humus in most soils has been protected from decomposition by microbial or enzyme action.
Protected humus is hidden (occluded) inside small aggregates of soil particles, or is tightly sorbed or complexed to clays.
Most humus that is not protected in this way is decomposed within 10 years.
Humus that is not protected in this way can be regarded as less stable or more labile.
Stable humus contributes few plant-available nutrients in soil.
Stable humus helps maintain the physical structure of soil.
A very stable form of humus is formed from the slow oxidation of soil carbon after finely powdered charcoal is incorporated into the topsoil.
The formation of the very stable humus from charcoal is speculated to have been important in the formation of the very fertile Amazonian terra preta do Indio.
